title: The Number That Appears Once Among Triples

concept.title: Count every bit position modulo 3: two bits per position are enough to remember a count from 0 to 2
body: In a list every value appears **exactly three times**, except one value that appears **once**. Find that value. For `2 2 3 2` it is 3, and for `0 1 0 1 0 1 99` it is 99. The trick that finds the single value among pairs (XOR of everything) does not work here, since `x ^ x ^ x = x`, not 0.

Look at **one bit position** at a time. Every value that appears three times contributes 0 or 3 ones to that position, so the **number of ones at the position, taken modulo 3, equals the bit of the single value**. That already gives a solution: for each of the 30 bit positions count the ones among all numbers and write `count % 3` into the answer. It costs 30 passes over the list.

body.code:
ones = twos = 0                 # for every bit: the count of ones modulo 3 is stored as (twos, ones)
for x in a:
    ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos     # the count 0 -> 1 -> 2 -> 0 ...
    twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones
print(ones)                       # the bits whose count is 1 modulo 3

body: The code above handles **all bit positions at once** with two numbers: `ones` and `twos` store, for each position, the count of ones modulo 3 as a two-bit counter (`00`, `01`, `10`). Adding a bit 1 moves the counter `00 -> 01 -> 10 -> 00`, which is what the two lines do for every position in parallel. After the whole list, every position of the repeated values is back at 0, and `ones` holds exactly the bits of the single value. One pass, O(n) time and O(1) memory.

statement: A list has `n` numbers. Every value appears exactly three times except one value, which appears exactly once. Print that value.
inputFormat: The first line has `n`: the number of values.
The second line has `n` numbers. Every value appears exactly three times except one value, which appears once.
outputFormat: Print the value that appears once.
constraints: 1 <= n <= 30000 and n = 3k + 1 for some k

examples.note: The value 2 appears three times, 3 appears once: 3.

hints: XOR does not cancel three equal values.
For one bit position, the number of ones modulo 3 is the bit of the answer.
Keep two bit masks, ones and twos, that count modulo 3 for all positions at once.

import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

# Your code here

explanation: Two masks store, for every bit position at once, the count of ones modulo 3; after all numbers the mask `ones` holds the bits of the value that appears once.

code.python:
import sys
input = sys.stdin.readline

n = int(input())
a = list(map(int, input().split()))

ones = twos = 0
for x in a:
    ones = (ones ^ x) & ~twos
    twos = (twos ^ x) & ~ones
print(ones)
